SMTO-GWT-0012 — The Gateway trusts a different SMTO than this one

GUID: ef3a8981-5267-42d6-9373-a5981b909e07
Slug: gateway-controller-changed
Domain: GWT · Subsystem: gateway

What happened

  • This Gateway remembers a different SMTO from the one now connecting, so it refused the request. Nothing was run on that computer.

How to fix — simple steps

  1. Check whether SMTO was recently reinstalled, moved to another computer, or started under a different user account. If so, start it the way it ran before. Each of these can give SMTO a new identity that the Gateway doesn't recognize.
  2. Ask the person who manages that computer, in person or by phone, whether another SMTO is meant to use this Gateway. If another SMTO owns it, replacing that link would cut it off.
  3. Only if they confirm this SMTO should take over, ask them to stop the Gateway, run its pairing reset command on that computer, and start it again. The Gateway never switches to a new SMTO on its own, to protect that computer.
  4. Open Settings › Setup › Gateways and select Check connection on that Gateway's row. After a reset, SMTO links to the Gateway automatically during this check.

What success looks like

  • The Gateway's row shows Connected and tasks run on it.

If it still fails

  • Select Copy error details and send them to the person who manages that Gateway. Don't reset the Gateway's pairing or turn off security checks just to make the connection work.

Technical details

Observed condition

  • The authenticated controller identity differs from the controller recorded in the Gateway's pairing, detected during request validation or the outbound handshake.

What this means

  • The authenticated controller identifier differs from the controller recorded in the Gateway pairing, either at request validation or outbound handshake. Use the retained operation phase and identity to determine effects; this explanation does not authorize retries or change pairing, target selection or execution ownership.

Why this can happen

  • The authenticated controller identifier differs from the controller recorded in the Gateway pairing, either at request validation or outbound handshake.

How to diagnose it

  • Compare the intended controller's public identity with the Gateway's pairing record and any deliberate controller migration.

How to fix it

  • Compare this Server's controller ID (key under ~/.smto/controller/identity or SMTO_CONTROLLER_STATE_DIR) with the controller_id in the Gateway's client-auth/pairing.json. If this Server's identity was lost or moved, restore the original key; only after confirming through a trusted channel that this Server should replace the paired one, reset pairing with the Gateway's local reset command and reconnect.
  • Verify the expected controller identity through a trusted channel before using the explicit pairing reset flow.

Retry and execution caution

  • Apply the correction and confirm the relevant state before requesting another attempt. Prior completed work remains governed by its receipts.

How to verify the fix

  • The expected controller authenticates under the preserved pairing or an explicitly verified replacement pairing.

What not to do

  • Do not automatically trust a replacement identity or disable certificate verification.

Technical notes

  • Use the retained operation phase and identity to determine effects; this explanation does not authorize retries or change pairing, target selection or execution ownership.
